79457269:
The standard does not specify the number, but I think it is reasonable to assume that it is a reasonable number. 
 For 32 bits processors I would expect it to be a 32 bit recursion (approx 4Billion) - that would not be achievable, as the stack used by 4 billion calls would consume all the memory of the processor. 
 For 64 bit machines, either 32 or 64 bits would be reasonable. 
 Algorithmically the recursive use of a mutex is problematic - if you think the potential recursions are > the number of bits on the processor (32 recursions / 64 recursions), then you probably need an alternative design - where the lock is held more globally and not used in inner functions. 
 The unspecified nature, allows the standard to be flexible, yet deliver something useful. If they specified a minimum size, that may limit the ability to implement C++ on some processors, due to the counter would need to be some form of atomic operation to work successfully.

The reason this works is because the inner lambda is non-capturing , so it is implicitly convertible to a C-style function pointer, which has no concept of object const-ness as there is no this parameter present. 
 The outer exec lambda sees that fn does not have a const function call operator, but it does have a const conversion operator, so exec is able to first convert fn into a function pointer, and then call it through that pointer. 
 Online Demo 
 If you add a capture to the inner lambda and then try to modify its value via mutable , the code will not compile as expected, eg: 
 int main()
{
 auto exec = []( auto const &fn ) { fn(); }; // <-- fails
 exec( [i=1]() mutable { i = 2; } );
}

 Since Perl supports foldings that are larger than the original, and since Perl's fc isn't language-aware, it returns the full case folding defined by Unicode. 
 Longer answer follows.

 The ideal fold of most Code Points is a single Code Point. These Code Points have a single common case folding (“C”). 
 Some Code Points have an ideal fold that consists of multiple Code Points. These Code Points have two foldings: the ideal but longer full case folding (“F”), and a single Code Point simple case folding (“S”). Implementations that want to avoid the complexities of folding into a larger sequence can opt to use the simple case folding instead of the full case folding . 
 But this one has three foldings! (The simple case folding is implied by the explicit definition of a full case folding .) Of all the Code Points, two have a special alternate folding rule. [1] This is one of them. 
 Of “T”, the notes in the file say: 
 
 special case for uppercase I and dotted uppercase I 
 
 For non-Turkic languages, this mapping is normally not used. 
 For Turkic languages (tr, az), this mapping can be used instead of the normal mapping for these characters. Note that the Turkic mappings do not maintain canonical equivalence without additional processing. See the discussions of case mapping in the Unicode Standard for more information. 
 
 Usage: 
 
 To do a simple case folding, use the mappings with status C + S. 
 
 To do a full case folding, use the mappings with status C + F. 
 The mappings with status T can be used or omitted depending on the desired case-folding behavior. (The default option is to exclude them.) 
 
 
 
 Having no sense of the language of the text, Perl must exercise the default option of excluding the Turkic case folding . 
 And since Perl put in the effort to support full case foldings , it returns this one.

79753103:
Yes. 
 The attributes are hints to the compiler for optimization. There are two main things that the compiler can do with this: 
 
 It can arrange the code so that the branch predictor's default choice (i.e. what to do if there's no history for the branch) takes the likely path. The common heuristic you hear about is that backwards branches (target instruction is earlier than branch instruction) are assumed to be taken (they look like loops, which are typically repeated more often than ended) and forward branches are assumed to not be taken. 
 
 It can put unlikely code far away from the likely code in a process called "outlining", so that the instructions that are unlikely to be executed anyway don't take up space in the instruction cache.

The lookup for T in T:: is defined as happening in the class first and as an unqualified lookup only if that finds nothing ([basic.lookup.qual.general]/3). That rule is, however, quite unsatisfying in cases like this: a template that works with types derived from one of its template parameters has no way of referring to that base class in a way that avoids collisions with members of the same name in the derived class. (A non-template could always use a fully qualified name for the base class.) 
 This has been the subject of a core issue for a long time, and I tried to change the rule , but it was CWG’s opinion that the adjacent . (or -> ) was just too important to look past (even only for dependent names). 
 The situation with ~T is even weirder, just because destructor “names” can successfully refer only to the type of the object expression or the nested name specifier. Here both qualified and unqualified lookup occur, but all that matters is that at least one matches that type, and obviously the qualified one will be the same as for T:: .

79788851:
Even if your question has been closed for obscure reasons, I want to say: it's a very interesting question about regex! 
 Most of the time, the goal of a validation regex is build to say if a string is conform to a format. It's a binary choice and doesn't give you more informations about where the format isn't conform in the string. 
 To find where the pattern fails, you have to build an always successful pattern where all characters on the right are optional. And to know at which character the pattern fails, you have to be able to know, where is the last successful character. To do that, you need to enclose each character into an optional capture group. 
 These optional capture groups have to be nested. 
 Example: 
 Your validation pattern is: 
 ^\d{2}/\d{2}/\d{2} \d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}$
 
 
 You have to write it like that: 
 ^(\d(\d(/(\d(\d(/(\d(\d( (\d(\d(:(\d(\d(:(\d(\d($)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?
 
 
 This way, you only have to check what capturing groups exist to know where the pattern fails. Obviously, C# gives you the offset of each capture group. 
 If you are interested on particular positions in the string, don't forget to use named capturing groups. 

 ^\d{2}/\d{2}/\d{2} \d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}$
 
 
 ^(\d(\d(/(\d(\d(/(\d(\d( (\d(\d(:(\d(\d(:(\d(\d($)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?)?
80009012:
Neither POSIX nor C FAQ recommend such a thing. 
 There are no POSIX APIs that take T const * const * so there's no need to cast anything to such type as far as POSIX is concerned. The quoted passage from the POSIX document explains why there are no such APIs, not what to do when you see one (there are none). 
 The quoted passage from the C FAQ doesn't mention such types at all. It does tell you that if you need to pass a char** to a function that expects const char** you would need a cast. This is hardly a recommendation, given that it immediately warns you that the need for such cast likely indicates a deeper problem that the cast wouldn't fix. 
 It is true that casting T ** to T const * const * (or indeed to T const ** ) and using the resulting pointer (even without modifying anything) can lead to UB, but there are no recommendations to use such casts by POSIX or C FAQ. 
 There is a problem of casting in the opposite direction though. Some APIs like execv expect a char * const * . If for some ungodly reason all you have is char const * const * , you need to cast (or copy the entire array, which to my limited knowledge nobody ever does). And this cast leads to the same sort of UB you describe. To clarify, the problem is an intermediate pointer being accessed through an lvalue of a type that is not a qualified version of the type of the underlying pointer object (one is T* and another is T const* , and no matter which is which, it's UB). 
 It is sometimes suggested that since T* and T const* have identical representation and alignment requirements, it is somehow OK to perform such access. But the standard makes no provision for that. 
 When programming in C, you shouldn't really be dealing with deeply qualified pointer types, precisely because they are broken and you cannot convert between those and nowhere-qualified pointers without UB. C and POSIX (to my knowledge) only use top-qualified multilevel pointers in their APIs so if you stick with their types, you should be fine. But the problem is there and it is known. 
 When writing in C++ it is harder to escape the problem because string literals are const . But in C, just avoid deep const . 
 For array types the problem is solved in C23: array types now share qualification with their element types, so you can now have multilevel const-qualified arrays and pointers to those arrays behave consistently. Pointers to pointers remain a problem though.
